fetched_contents.text: Removal of oil by walnut shell media Abstract Studies were conducted to evaluate the oil sorption capacities of walnut shell media. Sorption capacity is the weight of oil picked up by unit weight of a sorbent. Initial oil pick-up by walnut shell media on pure oil and oil on aqueous medium was evaluated. Batch kinetic studies were conducted to evaluate the equilibrium time required by walnut shell media for sorbing oil. For pure oil medium, sorption capacities of 0.30 g/g, 0.51 g/g and 0.58 g/g were obtained for standard mineral oil, vegetable oil and DoALL Bright-Edge oil, respectively. The results showed sorption capacities of 0.56 g/g, 0.58 g/g and 0.74 g/g for standard mineral oil, vegetable oil and DoALL Bright-Edge oil, respectively, for oil on aqueous medium. It was found that sorbed oil could be recovered from walnut shell media by applying pressure. The study showed that walnut shell media can be used as a sorbent for oil removal. Keywords Walnut shell media ; Pure oil ; Oil on aqueous medium ; Sorption capacity ; Oil removal Introduction Oils can cause environmental pollution during various stages of production, transportation, refining and use. Oils that are found in contaminated waters can be fats, lubricants, cutting liquids, heavy hydrocarbons such as tars, grease, crude oils, diesel oil, and light hydrocarbons such as kerosene, jet fuel and gasoline. Major industrial sources of oily waste include petroleum refineries, metal manufacturing and machining, and food processors. Sources of oil in municipal wastewater are kitchen and human wastes (Quemeneur and Marty, 1994). The best available technologies for oil removal include chemical treatment, gravity separation, parallel-plate coalescers, gas floatation, cyclone separation, granular media filtration and catridge filtration (Yang et al., 2002). Although many advanced technologies have been developed and applied in oily water treatment such as microfiltration (Hu et al., 2004) and ultra filtration (Lipp et al., 1998) membranes, the expensive initial and operating cost prohibited the wide application of these membrane filtration technologies. Deep-bed filtration is an attractive method to separate immiscible liquid from polluted wastewater. Many natural and synthetic media are available for treating oily waters. These media can be classified as filtering media (sand, coal, and diatomaceous earth), coalescing media (fiberglass, polypropylene) and adsorption media (activated carbon and peat). Crushed and/or processed plant materials have been used to adsorb oil from surfaces for some time. For example, cotton linters, crushed corncobs and modified pulp have been investigated (Johnson et al., 1973, Sun et al., 2002, Silva-Tilak, 2002). Deschamps et al. (2003) used cotton as a bed material to recover oil from oily water. They found that the oil–water separation could be improved at a lower temperature, lower flow, a deeper bed material and larger oil drop. Mathavan and Viraraghavan (1992) used horticultural peat as a bed material to examine the capability of the filter bed in oily water clean-up. Varghese and Cleveland (1998) studied the feasibility of using kenaf-filled filter in removing oil from a surfactant-stabilized oil-in water emulsion. The possibilities of reed canary grass, flax and hemp fiber as oil absorbing filter materials were investigated by Pasila (2004). It was found that these materials were able to separate oil from water during filtration of oily water. Ground walnut shell is a hard, chemically inert, nontoxic and biodegradable material mainly used as an abrasive. The shell makes up a large percentage of the nut (approximately 50%) and has a wide range of applications such as an ingredient in cosmetics and dental products, used for polishing and as a filtration medium (Hammons Product Co., 2007). Walnut shells are available in abundant supply as an agricultural byproduct of walnut-processing industry. Walnut shells are also advantageous because of their availability as a renewable resource. Walnut shell abrasive is used to blast clean and polish soft metals, fiberglass, wood, plastics and stone. It is an efficient soft abrasive when used to tumble and polish gun casings, jewelry, ink pens and metal parts (Hammons Product Co., 2007). Walnut shell serves as an effective filtration media when separating crude oil from water (Owens and Lee, 2007). Today, walnut shell filtration is used to treat oil field produced water, refinery wastewater, steel mill direct spray and caster water, ethylene plant quench water, copper concentrate decant and cooling water (Blumenschein et al., 2001). Walnut shells have been observed to have excellent surface characteristics for coalescing and filtration and superior resilience to attrition. Studies have been conducted to evaluate the use of walnut shell filters as an alternative to conventional sand filters to remove free oils and suspended solids (Blumenschein et al., 2001). USFilter Zimpro products, USA have developed an Auto-Shell Walnut shell filters to remove oily contaminants from water (USFilter Corporation, 2005). The walnut shell media is found to have good oil adsorbent ability and low media gravity (Yang et al., 2002). These have been observed to be tough enough to maintain their size during the back washing operation, thereby reducing possible loss during the filtration process (Rahman, 1992). Though studies are available on the use of walnut shell filters as an alternative to conventional sand filters, no information on its oil sorption capacity and oil recovery is available in the literature. Such a study would be useful to compare and select a sorbent for a particular application. The objective of this study was to evaluate the oil sorption capacity of walnut shell media. In the walnut fruit processing industry, large amounts of shells are produced as agricultural by-products and discarded or burned produced as fuel. Walnut (Juglans regia L.) is a valuable tree nut in the Juglandaceae family. The fruit is composed of four main parts: the kernel, the skin, the shell, and the husk. The importance of walnuts is mostly related to theirs valuable kernels. However, their shells are currently experiencing as much interest as their kernels due to the beneficial effects of the shells. In the past several years, walnut shell (WS) has been widely explored as a naturally inert plant-based biosorbent. In this review, we first highlight recent scientific literature regarding the development of adsorbents from WS in the form of carbon-based materials including unmodified/modified WS, and activated carbons (ACs). Next, we discuss the potential applications of WS-derived by-products as natural yet effective adsorbents for the removal of various hazardous materials including heavy metals (HMs), synthetic industrial dyes, and harmful chemicals. ---------------------------------------- The effective use of agricultural by-products is definitely a major challenge in waste management. 1. Introduction Currently, environmental contamination from various hazardous materials is a primary concern worldwide. It is a significant risk, and scientists believe that it endangers public health. For this reason, many recent studies have focused on the effective removal and elimination of such to reduce their harmful effects on living organisms.1 Annually, large amounts of toxic materials resulting from human industrial activities are discharged into the environment. Different synthetic dyes, various HM ions, oils derived from crude and processed petroleum, and pharmaceuticals are known to be significant hazardous compounds.2 Hazardous materials show carcinogenic and toxic effects, and thus is a growing interest worldwide for in the development of cost-effective, rapid, secure, regenerating and applicable biosorbents for the removal of such dangerous substances from industrial wastewaters before their discharge into terrestrial and aquatic ecosystems.3 Accordingly, the removal of different hazardous materials that threaten human health and affect various forms of life in aquatic ecosystems is now an important topic of study among environmental scientists. Currently, agricultural by-products and carbon-based products derived from waste crops seem to be the most attractive materials for the removal of various toxic chemicals because of their abundance, renewability, and cost-effectiveness. In recent years, various plant-based waste residues have been considered as adsorbents.4 Hazardous material separation using low-cost alternative adsorbents can be advantageous since provides a double advantage, i.e., waste product management and water purification. Additionally, the low-cost ACs derived from biomass similar or better than non-renewable coal-based granular activated carbons (GACs) and may successfully replace GACs. Consequently, the material used to produce ACs is critical because considerably affects the adsorption capacity. Nutshells, as standard and inexpensive agricultural waste materials, are used for this purpose.5 Walnut is as a popular tree nut that has been widely cultivated across the world for its valuable kernel. Inside the walnut fruit, the kernel is surrounded by three distinct layers called the seed coat, the shell, and the green husk. Unlike the kernel, the remaining parts of the fruit are regarded as waste products and are discarded without being put to any practical use.6 Recently, the walnut shell has gained increasing attention due to its high availability and several unique properties. One of the main and recently highlighted applications of WS by-products is the use of processed or unprocessed WS as biosorbent.7 Accordingly, this review aims to summarize up-to-date developments in the preparation and application of unmodified and modified WS in the form of ACs, as well as chemically modified WS in adsorption procedures for the removal of HMs, dyes, oils, pharmaceuticals and other hazardous substances from aqueous solutions. Additionally, important parameters for obtaining optimal adsorption conditions for different hazardous materials are highlighted. Furthermore, the thermodynamics of the adsorption reactions are discussed. Building upon the information derived from the literature review, concluding remarks and suggestions for future research are provided. 2. Ground walnut shells are effective for oil removal because their physical structure, chemical properties, and flow characteristics combine to create a favorable environment for oil capture. The most direct physical mechanism is the porous, capillary-rich structure of crushed walnut shells, which provides a large surface area and intricate network of tiny channels that force water through an arduous flow path. This structure enhances oil capture by trapping fine oil droplets and solids within the pore structure, while also increasing the adsorption area available for oil adhesion [N5-F2]. The same source also notes that walnut shells have a high modulus of elasticity and are light, which helps them resist attrition and maintain their structural integrity during backwashing [N5-F2].

Chemically, walnut shells are described as chemically inert, nontoxic, and biodegradable, with a surface chemistry that supports adsorption rather than absorption [N2-F1]. The material’s surface characteristics are especially important for oil removal, because the oil-water interaction occurs at the surface of the crushed nutshells, and the shell’s surface capillaries enable easy adhesion of oil to the surface [N5-F2]. The material is also noted as having low media gravity and being tough enough to maintain its size during backwashing, which is relevant to long-term performance but also indirectly supports adsorption efficiency by preserving the media structure [N2-F1]. The cited study on walnut shell media also reports sorption capacities of up to 0.74 g/g for aqueous oil systems, showing that the material can adsorb significant quantities of oil [N2-F1]. This suggests that hydrophobic interactions and surface adsorption, rather than dissolution, are the dominant mechanisms in oil removal.

Flow conditions and particle size affect removal efficiency because walnut shell media is designed to operate in deep-bed filtration, where a densely packed bed creates a tortuous flow path that increases contact time between water and media [N5-F2]. The source also specifies that walnut shell filters are typically used for feed concentrations up to 50 mg/L for both oil and solids, and that a maximum solids mean size of 5 microns is acceptable [N5-R1]. This indicates that smaller particles and lower concentrations are more compatible with deep-bed filtration, because the bed can more effectively trap fine oil droplets and solids without excessive clogging or pressure drop. The same source describes the filter as ideal for use downstream of hydrocyclones or flotation packages, implying that pretreatment reduces the burden on the deep-bed stage and improves efficiency [N5-F2]. The comparison in the walnut shell filter literature also notes that walnut shell filters are used as an alternative to conventional sand filters, which suggests that their performance depends on the upstream pretreatment and flow conditions rather than being inherently superior in all settings [N2-F1].

Overall, ground walnut shells are effective because their highly porous, capillary-rich structure maximizes contact and retention of oil droplets, their chemically inert and hydrophobic surface supports surface adsorption, and their deep-bed configuration, along with appropriate particle size and feed concentration, enhances removal efficiency [N5-F2][N2-F1][N5-R1].

Operational requirements for deep-bed use are therefore important. Feed concentration limits and particle size constraints are critical: walnut shell filters typically have a feed concentration limit of 50 mg/L for both oil and solids, and a maximum solids mean size of 5 microns [N5-R1]. Backwashing protocols are also important, as the evidence describes pressure-drop-triggered and time-based backwashing cycles, along with high-gravity backwashing aimed at improving regeneration capacity [N5-F2][N5-F3]. The evidence also implies that walnut shell filters are most suitable as polishing units installed downstream of hydrocyclones or flotation packages [N5-F2], which is an important practical consideration for integrating them into a broader treatment train.

## Evidence on regeneration, backwashing, and long-term viability

The evidence on regeneration, backwashing, and long-term viability shows that walnut shells can be regenerated effectively, but regeneration affects capacity and performance, and long-term stability depends on how well fouling is managed. The strongest direct evidence is that walnut shell media can be repeatedly used and restored [N2-R2]. Another source describes a high-gravity backwashing method aimed at improving the backwashing regeneration capacity of walnut shell filters [N5-F3], indicating that regeneration is not only possible but can be optimized with advanced techniques. The same source notes that the high-gravity backwashing process is designed to address problems such as poor regeneration of granular media, contamination of the filter bed, and low efficiency of oil/water separation [N5-F3]. This suggests that regeneration is an important means of restoring performance after fouling.

Backwashing or regeneration affects capacity and performance in several ways. First, backwashing is required to remove accumulated oil and solids from the packed bed, and the evidence states that oil remains entrapped and must be dislodged during backwashing [N5-F2]. Second, the pressure drop through the filters increases as oil and solids accumulate, and the automatic backwashing cycle is programmed to activate either by time or pressure drop [N5-F2]. This means that backwashing not only restores media function but also helps maintain the filter’s capacity by preventing excessive clogging. The evidence also notes that walnut shell media is not affected by heavy oil surges and is resistant to fluid fouling [N5-R2], which implies that regeneration is less burdensome than for some other media, but still necessary.

Long-term stability and fouling resistance are therefore shaped by both the media’s properties and the operational regime. The evidence indicates that walnut shells have a highly porous structure and a high modulus of elasticity, which helps them maintain their size and structural integrity during backwashing [N5-F2]. This structural resilience supports long-term stability by reducing attrition and preserving the media’s adsorptive capacity. At the same time, the evidence also shows that walnut shell filters are subject to fouling and pressure drop build-up, which requires regeneration and careful operation [N5-F2][N5-F3]. The high-gravity backwashing study further implies that long-term viability depends on improving regeneration efficiency rather than relying on a single cycle [N5-F3].

## Integrated conclusion

Ground walnut shells are an effective and renewable deep-bed filter media for removing oil from water because their highly porous, capillary-rich structure enhances oil capture and retention, their chemically inert and hydrophobic surface supports surface adsorption, and their deep-bed configuration improves contact time and removal efficiency [N5-F2][N2-F1]. At the same time, walnut shells are a renewable and sustainable choice because they are an abundant agricultural byproduct, their sourcing and processing carry low environmental costs, and they can be regenerated or reused, which reduces waste and resource consumption [N4-F4][N4-R5][N2-R2][N5-F3]. However, practical use comes with trade-offs: fouling, clogging, and capacity loss require backwashing and careful operation, and performance depends on feed concentration, particle size, and pretreatment [N5-F2][N5-R1][N6-R2]. Overall, walnut shells are well suited for oil removal in deep-bed systems when operated within their limits and regenerated effectively, making them a compelling choice for both effectiveness and sustainability [N5-F2][N2-R2][N5-F3].
